claims.text: The new predictive approach explicitly separates lattice and electronic heat transport in HfNbTaTiZr.
Incorporating atomic-scale disorder beyond perfect-crystal approximations will improve estimates of lattice thermal conductivity.
The approach will predict lower lattice thermal conductivity from 300 to 1200 K than prior perfect-crystal estimates.
Disorder-induced phonon scattering lowers the lattice thermal conductivity of HfNbTaTiZr.
Combining the predicted lattice contribution with independently measured electronic contributions will reproduce a total thermal conductivity of 10–17 W/(K m).
The model's improvement will be most pronounced at high temperatures.
The model's improvement will be most pronounced in samples with measurable oxygen content.
The target material is bulk polycrystalline HfNbTaTiZr containing 1 wt.% oxygen.
Atomic-scale disorder and oxygen impurities produce phonon scattering.
Phonon scattering in the model arises from mass disorder, force-constant variations, and impurity effects.
Accounting for mass disorder, force-constant variations, and impurity effects leads to a lower predicted lattice thermal conductivity than perfect-crystal models.
The new approach will improve prediction accuracy by at least 20–30% relative to prior analytical estimates.
Prior analytical and DFT-based estimates represent perfect crystals and omit disorder and impurity effects.
Prior analytical and DFT-based estimates tend to overestimate lattice thermal conductivity.
The prediction is applicable to bulk polycrystalline HfNbTaTiZr with 1 wt.% oxygen from 300 to 1200 K.
The prediction is not applicable to defect-free single crystals.
The prediction is not applicable below 200 K, where electronic and lattice thermal-conductivity contributions are comparable.

The hypothesis is falsified if predicted lattice conductivity combined with measured electronic conductivity fails to match measured total conductivity within 10%, or if the approach fails to outperform prior analytical estimates by at least 20%.
